title: Getting to the Bottom of Poor Performance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article challenges the default reach for a Performance Improvement Plan whenever an employee underperforms, arguing that PIPs quietly assume the problem is fully within the employee's control. The author offers a lengthy list of alternative root causes, from unclear manager expectations and conflicting feedback to psychological distraction and sabotage by others. The core message is that leaders need to diagnose the actual cause of underperformance before prescribing a fix, since a PIP may simply miss the real issue. The piece closes by acknowledging a PIP might still be the right tool -- but only after that diagnostic work is done.
points: Performance Improvement Plans quietly assume weak performance is fully within an employee's control, which isn't always true.
The article lists a wide range of alternative causes: unclear expectations, conflicting feedback, limited resources, sabotage, and personal distraction, among others.
Leaders should diagnose the actual root cause of underperformance before defaulting to a standard improvement plan.
A PIP may still be the right response in some cases, but only once the underlying issue has actually been identified.
quotes: Good leaders keep a sharp eye on performance metrics, team conversations, and third-party feedback to ascertain if a problem exists.
They presume that weak performance is within the perceived control of a given team member.
The team member believes faulty or limited resources inhibit performance
Simply setting short-term goals and milestones to confirm improvement without understanding the root issues underlying poor performance doesn’t get the job done.
Perhaps a Performance Improvement Plan is the best course of action. Then again, it might miss the boat entirely.
